Did you now that "Kustavi" in Swedish means "the vi at the coast".  What is a "vi" you might wonder? That is a old Norse name of a certain pre-christian cult site (often appere in a pattern of place names that signifies societal function wich includes names with Tuna, Lund and Karl as well as sometimes Ala and Hov). This is tge same element at the first in the name of the now Russian city of Vyborg (or Viborg in Swedish, as it was foynded by the Swedes). So: Kust = coast, -a- = plural genetive used in old compound words, -vi = pre-chridtisn cultsite.

Not sayin that the place "Kustavi" means that, or that it has that historical origin. However I do say that the name fits that meaning exactly in Swedish. Have no clue if it means something different in Finnish.

comments.author: @JeremiCzarnecki
comments.text:
Pretty much EVERY Baltic ferry between Finland and Sweden stops in Mariehamn.

Aland was able to keep itself a duty-free territory by a special accord despite both Finland and Sweden being members of the European Union, and they are able to keep sales of mostly alcohol untaxed or at least taxed lower than in either country.

This pretty much keeps the local economy afloat, as they can charge every ferry a port fee in return for said ferry to be able to do duty-free sales (the ferry doesn't have to be in Aland, it just has to be en route to or from Aland, most ferries call in Mariehamn for the briefest if moments).

Since alcohol sales are highly regulated and taxed in Sweden, and yet Swedes are notorious drunkards (which is why Sweden taxed and regulated alcohol in the first place), there is even a saying "to take the finlandsbåt" (a ferry to Finland), referring to a short cruise, oftentimes not even involving going ashore, to Finland and back, with the objective to get drunk and party hard.

So your best bet is actually taking one of the multiple daily departures from the major ports of Sweden or Finland and be the weird person actually alighting in the middle of the night in Mariehamn.

You can also time your travels to coincide with the three days a week Finnair runs a flight from Helsinki or have the dubious pleasure of flying with the local airline Populair, which operates tiny Fokker 50 flights between Arlanda and Turku with a stop in Mariehamn.

Finnair isn't much better, as they outsource the Aland flights to NORRA, one of the last operators of ATR turboprops in the developed world, as both the passenger volumes and the runway are too small for most jets.

The good news is that flights are shorter than an hour.

Getting from Mariehamn to the other Islands is not that much of a problem either - the most populous ones are only technically separate from Fasta and connected by bridges, while the outer ones, closer to mainland Finland, have regular ferries between them and sometimes even directly between the island and the mainland (mostly Turku).

Unless you REALLY want to try to reach the remotest of Islands, this is not nearly as hardcore as the Faroe Islands, even if the population of Aland is actually quite a bit smaller than Faroese.
